Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Rosa’s shift on October fourteenth began normally, the diesel hum vibrating through her boots as she navigated Elm Street. A red sedan fishtailed, then slammed into a delivery truck. Rosa’s brakes locked, but momentum carried her forward until she only barely missed the wreckage. Through the windshield, she watched a man slump over the wheel, dark blood spreading across the hood and dripping onto the pavement. She tried to push the door open, but her hands trembled so violently she could not grip the handle. She stood there until responders arrived, yet the helplessness of that moment—the way her body refused to obey, the way she could only watch—settled into her bones. In the weeks that followed, the memory returned as a sudden, total immersion. During a layover, the sensation of wet asphalt and the sharp tang of blood flooded her senses at once, as if she were standing at the intersection again. Other times, it came without a picture—a raw panic that settled in her chest, identical to the fear she felt when the sedan lost control. The boundary between then and now dissolved entirely. When traffic slowed at a merge lane, her grip tightened, convinced that if she did not maintain absolute command of the pedals, another collapse would follow. She began silently counting her breaths in threes, reciting verses under her breath, or tapping her fare box exactly seven times before closing the door. She was certain that if she stopped the counting, or broke the rhythm, the intersection would happen again on her route. Rosa’s routes grew narrower. She avoided looking out side windows when other vehicles drifted too close, fixating on the rearview mirror instead. When passengers reached for the handrail, she flinched at the brush of fabric, pulling her arms inside her jacket. She would not let anyone sit beside her in the break room, claiming she needed space for her logs. She steered clear of folded funeral programs and quiet corners where names of the dead were mentioned. At home, she turned her body away when her husband rested his hand on her shoulder, saying she was tired. The distance between them grew quiet. The thought that she would never forgive herself for not doing more, that she had failed to protect those in that car, and that she was not sure her life was worth living anymore lingered constantly. At sixty-one, Rosa’s sleep fractured. Some mornings, she woke with her heart hammering, certain she had heard the crash in her bedroom. Her supervisor pulled her aside after she missed two layovers and refused the northbound line, noting how she had begun rerouting around familiar stops to avoid seeing other cars. The shift schedule had been cut. Unpaid hours accumulated alongside a quiet dread that followed her into the grocery store, where the sharp sight of red taillights made her step into the parking lot aisle and press her back against a concrete pillar until the sensation faded. What brought her to this clinic was the exhaustion of the counting, the silence in her passenger seat, and the realization that she no longer wanted to drive through the streets where the memories waited. She came hoping someone might help her stop waiting for the next wreck, wondering if the weight of what she had witnessed could finally be put down.
